analysis.one_liner: Caps House campaign spending at $600,000 per cycle in exchange for public campaign vouchers.
analysis.headline: The House passed campaign spending limits with public vouchers 255-175, but the bill was tabled in favor of a Senate companion that never cleared a Senate filibuster, and it never became law.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill set up a voluntary program for House races: a candidate who agreed to spend no more than $600,000 in an election cycle could receive up to $200,000 in public "voter communication vouchers" to pay for ads and mail, funded through a Treasury fund with no net cost to the Treasury [S3][S4]. It capped contributions from political committees and large donors at $200,000 each per cycle, banned contribution bundling through intermediaries, barred national party committees from raising unregulated "soft money," and required broadcasters to sell candidates ad time at the lowest rate and not bump those ads [S3][S4]. Limits were waived if a nonparticipating opponent outspent the thresholds, and the bill itself provided for expedited Supreme Court review, acknowledging that the spending caps faced constitutional doubt [S4].
analysis.who_benefits: Candidates without big-donor and PAC networks, especially challengers and first-time candidates, who could run competitive races on small contributions matched by public vouchers; and voters, whose candidates would be less financially dependent on large donors and lobbyists.

how_it_helps.text: An eligible House candidate could receive up to $200,000 in vouchers, matched to small individual contributions (up to $200 per person), with extra vouchers if independent expenditures were spent against them, reducing reliance on large checks [S3][S4].

The bill prohibited anyone from acting as a conduit or intermediary bundling contributions to a candidate and capped aggregate political-committee and large-donor contributions at $200,000 per cycle, limiting the fundraising machine of incumbent officeholders [S3][S4].

National party committees were barred from soliciting or accepting contributions not subject to federal limits, closing the soft-money channel used to pour unregulated money into federal elections [S3][S4].

Broadcasters had to make time available to House candidates in the 45 days before a general election at the lowest unit charge and could not preempt those ads, and candidates had to put their own voice on ads, making campaign communication cheaper and more accountable [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Large donors, PACs, and lobbying interests that lose the influence built through big checks and bundling; national party committees lose their soft-money pipeline; broadcasters give up some premium ad rates; and the voucher program is funded through a Treasury fund, with the bill requiring budget neutrality [S3][S4].

drawbacks.text: The spending cap ($600,000 per cycle) is low enough that critics worried it could shield incumbents, who are already known to voters, while starving challengers who need money just to introduce themselves; the bill also let limits collapse entirely whenever a nonparticipating opponent exceeded 25 percent of the cap [S4].

The bill's own expedited-Supreme-Court-review provision shows its drafters expected the expenditure limits to face constitutional challenge under the ruling that spending limits cannot be imposed on candidates who refuse them; a voluntary cap with waivers can be evaded by the best-funded campaigns [S4].
The final House version dropped the companion spending limits and benefits for Senate races, leaving the Senate side to a separate bill that never passed [S3].

The Senate side of the program was stripped out of the final bill, so Senate campaigns, where costs are highest, would have remained outside the spending-limit system in the House-passed version [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: A genuine, broad attempt to shrink the role of big money in House elections, but a deliberately weak one: participation was voluntary, limits fell away the moment an opponent opted out, and the Senate was left to a companion bill. The structural complaint that caps favor incumbents is a fair one. The core gains, public vouchers matched to small donors, a bundling ban, and a soft-money ban, would have meaningfully reduced dependence on large contributors.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it 255-175 on November 22, 1993, but immediately laid it on the table in favor of the Senate's companion bill, and the Senate never got that companion past a blocking minority, so the Congress ended with no campaign reform law.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on January 5, 1993, as an early priority of the new Democratic House majority [S6].

The House Administration Committee marked it up and ordered it reported 12-7 on November 10, 1993, and it passed the House on November 22 by 255-175, with Democrats voting 232-24 in favor and Republicans 22-151 against [S6][S7].
A Republican motion to recommit the bill to committee was defeated 190-240 (Democrats 25-231 against the motion, Republicans 165-8 for it) [S7].
On passage, the House laid the bill on the table with instructions to take up the Senate companion, S. 3, as the vehicle for further action [S6].
The Senate companion never became law; Senate Republicans blocked it through the end of the 103rd Congress, and no campaign spending-limit bill was enacted [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large donors, PACs, and party soft-money operations kept the campaign finance system they knew, and incumbent members kept their fundraising advantage; no campaign reform was enacted.

for.name: Sam Gejdenson
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on January 5, 1993, and recruited 45 cosponsors.

for.name: 232 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Voted 232-24 for final passage on November 22, 1993, and 231-25 to reject the motion to recommit.

for.name: House Administration Committee (Democratic majority)
for.role: Committee with jurisdiction over election law
for.what_they_did: Held a markup on November 10, 1993, and reported the bill 12-7.

for.name: Bill Clinton
for.what_they_did: Made congressional campaign finance reform a top legislative priority and pushed Congress to pass it.

against.name: 151 House Republicans
against.what_they_did: Voted 151-22 against final passage, and 165-8 for the motion to recommit the bill to committee.

against.name: Tillie Fowler
against.what_they_did: Moved to recommit the bill to the House Administration Committee, a procedural move to delay or defeat it.

against.name: Senate Republicans
against.what_they_did: Blocked the Senate companion bill (S. 3), the designated vehicle for the reform, from ever reaching an up-or-down vote.

sides.party_line_note: Final passage split 232-24 among Democrats and 22-151 among Republicans; the failed motion to recommit showed the reverse split (Democrats 25-231, Republicans 165-8).

industries.industry: Political action committees and large donors
industries.note: The bill capped their aggregate contributions to a House candidate at $200,000 per cycle and banned bundling through conduits, sharply reducing their leverage over members. Their gain under the status quo is the public's cost in policy independence.

National party committees were barred from soliciting or accepting contributions not subject to federal limits, shutting the unregulated soft-money channel. The parties' interest in keeping that pipeline ran against the transparency the bill offered voters.

The bill shortened the lowest-unit-rate window, banned preemption of candidate ads, and let vouchers pay for airtime, cutting some premium ad revenue while creating a guaranteed voucher-funded market. A modest revenue trade-off, not a core fight.

The bundling ban and contribution caps cut into members' fundraising machines, but low spending caps can favor candidates already known to voters, and the passed bill's incumbents wrote the design. House incumbents of both parties split along party lines rather than against the bill as a bloc.
